item.title: Guide to Teaching with Data in Statistics and Data Science Classrooms
item.description: arXiv:2611.00470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistics and data science educators have been concerned about data use or lack thereof in the classroom for decades. For many educators, the question is not whether to use data or not. They often want to know whether they should give clean or messy data, and whether they should spend the time to find a real dataset or simulate it. If they decide to find real data, then other questions follow about where to find it and how to provide it to students. If they provide data, then the question remains whether students will find the data engaging or not or if it will have the properties necessary to demonstrate class concepts. We provide empirically and theoretically supported recommendations on data use. Classroom data are described in different ways (e.g., real, raw, made-up, artificial, fictitious, synthetic, simulated, toy, and messy). We provide definitions of different types, sources, formats, and shapes of data and provide distinctions between classifications. We share resources for educators in bringing data to their classrooms.
item.dc:creator: Mine Do\u{g}ucu, Catalina Medina, Crystal Lewis

item.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Development: Building Rigorous, Decision-Ready Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.00557v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the pharmaceutical lifecycle, from discovery and clinical development through manufacturing and regulatory review to safety surveillance and health economics, creating evidentiary challenges that predictive performance alone cannot address. This review examines the inferential, causal, validation, and documentation requirements for AI-enabled evidence generation in high-stakes settings and argues that they must be built into workflows. We outline the evidentiary functions that AI-derived outputs must satisfy before supporting consequential decisions: estimand definition, fit-for-purpose data collection, bias control, uncertainty quantification, validation, interpretability, and decision-grade documentation. Because AI both depends on and accelerates large-scale, non-randomized data collection, the integration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with real-world data (RWD) is where its evidentiary risks concentrate; we therefore present a five-step causal roadmap for that integration, in which external data supplement but never replace a concurrent control, and characterize the safeguards required across development, pharmacovigilance, regulation, and health technology assessment. Priority frontiers answer recurring implementation problems: conformal prediction for overconfident predictions, randomization-based inference for scarce data, and federated causal inference and privacy-preserving generative modeling for data that cannot be pooled. Evidence generation depends not on competition between RCTs and RWD, or between statistics and AI/ML, but on their principled synthesis under causal and inferential frameworks, with statistical expertise central to decision-ready evidence.
item.dc:creator: Xin Luo, Margaret Gamalo, Achilleas Livieratos, Maria Kudela, Qilu Yu, Yunxun Wang, Junjing Lin, Yuxi Zhao, Allshine Chen

item.title: Exploiting Locally Exogeneous Variation in Spatial Data: Linear Regression with Many Small Units
item.description: arXiv:2611.01854v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article shows how researchers can exploit \textit{locally exogeneous variation} even in the presence of endogeneity, autocorrelation, or spurious correlation. It describes the infill asymptotic properties of generalized least squares estimation with county-level data, Census tract-level data, and similar regional averages, including sufficient conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality, and valid inference.
item.dc:creator: Christopher W. Engh

item.title: PLS-SEM-power: A Shiny App and R package for Computing Required Sample Size and Minimum Detectable Effect Size in PLS-SEMs
item.description: arXiv:2511.14546v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite its evanescent nature, statistical power is crucial for planning Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) studies. This brief paper introduces PLS-SEM-power, a Shiny Application and R package that implements the inverse square root method by Kock and Hadaya (2018) to calculate both the minimum required sample size (a priori analysis) and the Minimum Detectable Effect Size (MDES, sensitivity analysis), given a chosen significance level (alpha level) and desired statistical power (1 - beta), set to 0.80 by default. The software supports both one-tailed and two-tailed calculations, with one-tailed calculations as the default following the formulation of Kock and Hadaya (2018), and provides an intuitive user interface, facilitating reproducible and easily accessible analyses in diverse research contexts.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Ansani

item.title: Network Analysis in Communication Research: A Review of Methods, Theories, and Research Practices
item.description: arXiv:2609.30905v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Network analysis has become a standard way of representing consultation, sourcing, media use, attention, and influence in communication research. This review examines 31 applications across communication subfields and asks of each what communication problem it addresses, which explanatory resource it invokes, and what its research practice makes observable. The three dimensions form a comparison framework and yield three propositions with stated scope and refutation conditions: resource relevance is task- and criterion-dependent; commonality at one level of aggregation does not imply commonality at another; and influence estimates are conditional on relationship type, group stage, and time. A short bibliometric section describes how the literature's cited references are organised: method references are paired with one another more often than year-specific margins predict (ratio 1.36) and with theoretical references less often (0.82), a pattern consistent with a methodological toolkit that circulates apart from the commitments that license its use. The review closes with designs that would test each proposition.
item.dc:creator: Pengjia Cui
